title: Choosing and using an equation
learning_outcomes: List u, v, a, s and t for one straight-line constant-acceleration interval, including signs and units.
Choose an equation that contains the target and known quantities but avoids an unnecessary unknown.
Rearrange, substitute and report a physically meaningful result with units and direction.
prior_knowledge_summary: From 9702_t02_cm03_l06, students know the three registered equations and that they apply to straight-line motion with constant acceleration.
From 9702_t02_cm03_l06, students can identify u, v, a, s and t and know that signs follow a chosen positive direction.
From 9702_t02_cm02_l05, students can use signed velocity-time area to find displacement.
new_learning: A systematic known-target-unwanted routine for choosing an equation.
Check units, sign and physical sense after calculating.
not_yet_taught: Free fall and vertical sign conventions

inside_scope: One straight-line interval with constant acceleration
Direct calculation of one target from supplied knowns

evidence_basis.evidence_summary: Mapped parts require selecting or rearranging a relation, substituting in SI units and reporting a direct numerical result. The lesson stays with one interval and supplies original contexts and values.
evidence_basis.canonical_audit: Checked all canonical direct-calculation parts and mark schemes. They support concise relation selection, rearrangement, SI substitution and reporting, while their later-topic contexts are not copied.
evidence_basis.scope_note: Projectile, pendulum and free-fall contexts in mapped evidence are excluded; only the one-interval calculation procedure is reused.

visual_rules.style: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch with basic annotations, visible pencil texture and only essential labels.
visual_rules.reason: Six visuals support the opening choice, the selection routine, signs, rearrangement, checking and synthesis using varied visual forms.

blocks.title: Three equations, one useful choice
body: A test trolley starts at 3.0 m s^-1 and accelerates at 2.0 m s^-2 for 4.0 s. We want its displacement.
Prediction: which equation gets us there without first finding another quantity?
All three equations are valid, but one route is shorter because it does not contain final velocity v.

figure.purpose: Make equation choice visible as a route-selection problem.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn trolley with cards for u, a and t, a question-mark card for s, and three equation signposts. Lightly cross out the route containing v without revealing the numerical answer.
figure.alt_text: A trolley's known quantities and target are connected to three possible equation routes.

blocks.title: Build a five-letter snapshot
body: First choose one interval. Then write u, v, a, s and t in a small table.
Put in each known value with its sign and unit. Mark the quantity you need with a question mark. Leave every other unknown blank.
For the trolley: u = 3.0 m s^-1, a = 2.0 m s^-2, t = 4.0 s, s = ?, and v is blank.
The blank matters. It tells us which equation would introduce an unnecessary unknown.

figure.purpose: Teach the known-target-unwanted classification before formula selection.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn five-row u-v-a-s-t table. Use ticks for u, a and t, a target circle for s, and a blank warning triangle for v. Include units beside knowns.
figure.alt_text: A five-row table separates known quantities, the target displacement and the unwanted final velocity.

blocks.title: Choose the equation that avoids the blank
body: These are formulas to remember. They model straight-line motion with constant acceleration.
Look for an equation that contains the target and the knowns, but not the unwanted blank.
Here s is the target, u, a and t are known, and v is unwanted. The displacement equation is the direct route.
symbols_and_units: u is initial velocity in m s^-1.
v is final velocity in m s^-1.
a is constant acceleration in m s^-2.

figure.purpose: Show equation selection by variable membership rather than guesswork.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn comparison grid with the three equations as rows and u, v, a, s, t as columns. Circle the row containing u, a, s and t but no v.
figure.alt_text: A variable grid shows which quantities appear in each constant-acceleration equation.

blocks.title: Walk the trolley calculation through
body: Use s = ut + 1/2 at^2 because it contains s, u, a and t but not v.
Substitute only after the equation is chosen: s = (3.0)(4.0) + 1/2(2.0)(4.0)^2.
The first term gives 12 m. The second gives 16 m. So s = 28 m.
The positive result means 28 m in the chosen positive direction. The unit is metres because displacement was the target.

figure.purpose: Model a clean written calculation with meaning attached to each line.
figure.brief: Annotated hand-written layout with four aligned lines: equation, substitution, arithmetic and signed result with unit. Small side notes label select, substitute, calculate and interpret.
figure.alt_text: An annotated four-line calculation finds the trolley displacement as 28 metres.

blocks.title: A minus sign is information
body: Suppose right is positive and a trolley moves right at 8.0 m s^-1 while slowing at 2.0 m s^-2. Its acceleration is a = -2.0 m s^-2.
It can feel natural to write every given magnitude as positive. That works only when every vector points in the positive direction.
Using v = u + at gives v = 8.0 + (-2.0)(3.0) = 2.0 m s^-1. The trolley still moves right after 3.0 s.
If the minus sign were lost, the calculation would describe speeding up, which is a different motion.

figure.purpose: Connect algebraic signs to physical directions and expose the all-positive misconception.
figure.brief: Two-panel vector sketch. In the correct panel, velocity arrow points right and acceleration arrow left. In the mistaken panel both arrows point right. Add a positive-right axis.
figure.alt_text: A comparison shows that a slowing trolley has velocity and acceleration in opposite directions.

blocks.title: Rearrange before numbers arrive
body: Now a cart changes from 5.0 m s^-1 to 11.0 m s^-1 over 24 m. We need acceleration and time is unknown.
Choose v^2 = u^2 + 2as because it contains v, u, a and s but no t.
Rearrange with symbols first: a = (v^2 - u^2) / (2s). Then substitute: a = (11.0^2 - 5.0^2) / (2 x 24) = 2.0 m s^-2.
Symbolic rearrangement keeps the structure visible and makes misplaced squares easier to spot.

figure.purpose: Show the difference between rearranging symbols and inserting numbers too early.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn balance-style algebra sequence from v squared equals u squared plus 2as to a isolated. Beside it, a tidy substitution line and a crossed-out cluttered numbers-first line.
figure.alt_text: A symbolic algebra sequence isolates acceleration before values are substituted.

blocks.title: A different route: find stopping time
body: A cyclist moves right at 12.0 m s^-1 and brakes with constant acceleration -3.0 m s^-2. We need the stopping time.
Choose right as positive. At rest, v = 0 m s^-1, so u = +12.0 m s^-1, a = -3.0 m s^-2 and t is the target.
Use v = u + at and rearrange before substituting: t = (v - u) / a.
t = (0 - 12.0) / (-3.0) = 4.0 s. Both negative signs are necessary. The positive time is physically sensible.
Independent check: the speed falls by 3.0 m s^-1 each second, so four one-second drops take 12.0 m s^-1 to zero.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in a different route: find stopping time visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for a different route: find stopping time.

blocks.title: Use the K-T-U-S-C check
body: Knowns: list values with signs and units for one interval.
Target: mark the quantity to find.
Unwanted: notice the quantity that is neither known nor needed.
Select and solve: choose the equation without the unwanted quantity, rearrange, then substitute.
Check: give the unit, interpret the sign and ask whether the size fits the motion.
The opening trolley needed displacement, not final velocity. Choosing s = ut + 1/2 at^2 made 28 m a direct result instead of a two-step detour.

concepts_taught: Equation choice follows from known, target and unwanted quantities.
Signs encode direction and must be fixed before substitution.
Symbolic rearrangement should precede numerical substitution.
A result needs a unit, sign interpretation and physical-sense check.
misconceptions_addressed: Any valid equation is equally direct.
All supplied magnitudes should be entered as positive.
Numbers should be substituted before rearranging.
A bare number is a complete physical answer.
skills_students_can_now_use: List signed knowns and units for one interval.
Choose an equation that avoids an unnecessary unknown.
Rearrange any of the three registered equations for a direct target.
Substitute, calculate and interpret a result.
